Danger Signs During Delivery: If you or your baby experience any of the following, seek immediate medical attention at a hospital or health center, regardless of the time of day or night. Do not delay: For the mother: If the water breaks and labor does not start within 6 hours. If labor pains (contractions) persist for more than 12 hours. If there is heavy bleeding (soaking more than 2-3 pads in 15 minutes). If the placenta is not expelled within 1 hour after the baby is born. For the baby: If the baby is very small. If there is difficulty breathing. If the baby has seizures (fits). If the baby has a fever or feels cold. If there is bleeding or the baby is unable to feed. Routine Postnatal Contacts: If the birth occurs at home, the first postnatal contact should be within 24 hours of delivery. The second contact should occur on day 3 (48-72 hours after birth). The third contact should take place between days 7 and 14 after birth. A final postnatal clinic visit should occur at 6 weeks postpartum. Care During Pregnancy: Visit a health worker as soon as you suspect you are pregnant to begin early prenatal care. The health worker will guide you on when to return for follow-ups. If you have any concerns about your health or your baby’s health, visit the health center immediately. During prenatal visits, the health worker will: Monitor your health and the progress of your pregnancy. Help you create a birth plan. Address any questions or concerns. Provide treatment for conditions like malaria and anemia. Administer tetanus toxoid immunizations. Offer advice on breastfeeding, birth spacing, nutrition, HIV counseling and testing, and other health matters. Always bring your home-based maternal record to every visit. Self-Care During Pregnancy: Eat a nutritious diet with plenty of fruits, vegetables, beans, meat, fish, eggs, and dairy products. Take iron tablets and any other prescribed supplements or medications daily as directed by your health worker. Rest when possible and avoid lifting heavy objects. Sleep under an insecticide-treated bed net to prevent malaria. Avoid alcohol, smoking, and any unprescribed medications. Use condoms correctly during sexual activity to prevent sexually transmitted infections (STIs) or HIV if you or your partner are at risk. When to Seek Care for Danger Signs During Pregnancy: Go to a hospital or health center immediately if you experience: Vaginal bleeding. Convulsions or fits. Severe headaches with blurred vision. Fever and extreme weakness. Severe abdominal pain. Rapid or difficult breathing. Preparing a Birth and Emergency Plan: Discuss your birth plan with your health worker at every visit. The plan may need to change if complications arise. Prepare a clean, warm room with necessary supplies, including clean cloths, a delivery kit, and warm covers. For emergencies, plan where to go, how to get there, and how to cover transportation and medical costs. Arrange for someone to accompany you and care for your home and children while you are away. Care for the Mother After Birth: Eat a healthy diet with more meat, fish, oils, nuts, cereals, vegetables, and fruits. Take iron tablets as prescribed. Rest and drink plenty of clean, safe water. Sleep under an insecticide-treated bed net. Avoid alcohol, smoking, and unprescribed medications. Use condoms during sexual activity if at risk of STIs or HIV. Wash daily, especially the perineum, and change sanitary pads every 4-6 hours. Family Planning After Birth: You can become pregnant within weeks after delivery if you are not exclusively breastfeeding. Use a family planning method to prevent unintended pregnancies. Care for the Baby After Birth: Keep your baby clean by washing their face and neck daily and bathing them as needed. Dry them thoroughly after bathing and keep them warm. Wash the baby’s bottom when soiled and dry it thoroughly. Wash your hands with soap and water before and after handling the baby, especially after changing diapers. Keep the umbilical cord stump clean and dry. Apply 1% chlorhexidine digluconate daily for the first week of life if recommended. Do not apply any other substances to the stump. Breastfeeding: Breastfeed exclusively for the first 6 months. Breast milk provides all the nutrients and water your baby needs and protects against infections and allergies. Begin breastfeeding within 1 hour of birth. Let the baby feed as often and as long as they want, day and night. Drink plenty of clean, safe water while breastfeeding. When to Seek Care for the Baby: Seek immediate medical attention if your baby: Has difficulty breathing. Feeds less than every 5 hours or stops feeding. Has yellow eyes or skin. Has pus or blood around the umbilical cord. Feels cold, has a fever, or is bleeding. Records and Forms: Maintain accurate records for monitoring labor, delivery, and postpartum care. These records are essential for tracking maternal and newborn health and ensuring proper follow-up care.
